hypotheses.hypothesis: Among player aggregates, dark-skinned players—defined as having a mean skin-tone score of at least 0.50—have a higher exposure-adjusted rate of straight reds plus second yellows than light-skinned players, estimated with an exposure-only Poisson mean model and model-based standard errors.
hypotheses.rationale: The player-aggregate and player-referee-dyad analyses produced materially different effects and inference, so the observational unit must be fixed. The exposure-only specification also provides a distinct, explicitly defined mean-model question. The sending-off definition, skin-tone rule, and standard-error method are pinned to make the claim testable; the multiverse evidence does not establish that these operational choices are uniquely preferable.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Among player-referee dyads, dark-skinned players—defined as having a mean skin-tone score of at least 0.50—have a higher exposure-adjusted rate of straight reds plus second yellows than light-skinned players, estimated with an exposure-only Poisson mean model and model-based standard errors.
hypotheses.rationale: This isolates the player-referee-dyad question from the player-aggregate question. The analysis-unit sensitivity was large, including sign and inference reversals, so these cannot be treated as one claim. The remaining decisions are fixed for a testable comparison using the existing dataset.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Among player aggregates, dark-skinned players—defined as having a mean skin-tone score of at least 0.50—have a higher exposure-adjusted rate of straight reds plus second yellows than light-skinned players, estimated with a Poisson mean model adjusted for player and league and model-based standard errors.
hypotheses.rationale: This asks the player-aggregate question under explicit adjustment for player and league rather than the exposure-only mean model. Mean-model specifications materially changed effect estimates and inference, particularly when comparing exposure-only with player-and-league adjustment, warranting a separate successor rather than a hedged claim.
